name: Idempotency
summary: Reprocessing the same input yields the same result — no duplicates, so retries and reruns are safe.
description: Idempotency guarantees that applying the same input more than once has the same effect as applying it once. It is the property that makes retries, restarts, and at-least-once delivery safe: a re-delivered record or a re-run batch converges to the same state rather than inserting duplicates. It is achieved with deterministic or natural keys, MERGE/upsert sinks, primary-key dedup, exactly-once sinks, and transactional table formats. It is strongest in warehouse/lakehouse MERGE and CDC upserts, and a trade-off in append-only logs where duplicates are possible and must be de-duplicated downstream.

mechanisms.name: Deterministic / natural keys
mechanisms.note: Deriving a stable key from the record's own content means the same input always maps to the same row, so a re-processed record overwrites rather than duplicates.

mechanisms.name: MERGE / upsert sinks
mechanisms.note: Writing with MERGE INTO on a key updates existing rows and inserts new ones, so re-running a batch converges to the same table state without duplicates.

mechanisms.name: Primary-key deduplication
mechanisms.note: De-duplicating on a primary key at read or write time absorbs duplicate deliveries from at-least-once sources into a single logical record.

mechanisms.name: Exactly-once / transactional sinks
mechanisms.note: Two-phase-commit or transactional writes tie output to committed input positions so a retried write is not double-applied.

mechanisms.name: Transactional table formats
mechanisms.note: ACID commits on open table formats make a write atomic and repeatable — a retried commit either lands once or not at all, never partially twice.

manifestations.statement: CDC applies changes as key-based upserts, so re-delivering the same change or re-running from an earlier offset converges the mirror to the same current state without duplicating rows.
Silver and gold typically MERGE on business keys into transactional tables, so re-running a batch is idempotent by construction and safe to retry after any failure.
ACID MERGE on stable keys plus atomic snapshot commits mean a retried write either lands once or not at all, giving strong out-of-the-box idempotency.
Incremental models keyed with unique_key perform MERGE-style upserts, so re-running a model reconciles to the same rows and duplicate source loads are absorbed on key.
Warehouse-native MERGE and dbt's unique-key incrementals make transformations idempotent, so re-running after a failed load produces the same table without double-counting.
Golden-record survivorship deterministically resolves the same inputs to the same master record, so re-processing a source contribution converges rather than forking new duplicate masters.
Dimension loads upsert on natural keys idempotently, but naive append-style fact loads can double-count on rerun unless guarded by a load key or delete-insert-by-partition pattern.
Idempotency is achievable via delete-insert-by-partition or MERGE, but it is a design choice per job; plain append loads are not idempotent and a rerun duplicates the batch.
Transactional commits give idempotent table writes, and upsert modes dedupe on key; still, achieving true end-to-end exactly-once requires the source, processor, and sink to cooperate.
Identity resolution upserts profiles on resolved keys, so re-ingesting a source is usually idempotent; ambiguous or changing match keys can occasionally split or merge profiles differently on rerun.
Offline feature tables upsert on entity+timestamp keys idempotently, but online writes to a low-latency store may be last-write-wins, so out-of-order retries can momentarily set a stale value.

Idempotency matters most here — double-sending an email or record is user-visible — so syncs upsert on a destination key and diff against last-synced state; safety depends on the destination honoring the key.

Stores like ClickHouse offer replacing/aggregating engines that dedupe on key eventually, giving practical idempotency, though duplicates can be briefly visible before background merges reconcile them.
At-least-once delivery is the default, so duplicates are possible; exactly-once requires transactional sinks and keyed dedup, trading some latency and throughput for idempotent output.
Durable logs favor at-least-once delivery for availability, so consumers must be written to dedupe on an idempotency key; the log itself does not guarantee once-only processing.
High-throughput append-only ingestion accepts duplicate events as the cost of speed, pushing de-duplication downstream into aggregation or a dedup pass rather than the ingest path.
Devices retransmit on flaky networks, so at-least-once duplicates are routine; idempotency is recovered downstream by deduping on device-id plus event-time rather than at the edge.
Append-only file landing offers no key semantics, so re-running an ingest drops duplicate files; idempotency has to be imposed entirely by downstream readers deduping on content.

tradeoffs.title: Throughput
tradeoffs.note: Deduplication, MERGE, and upsert bookkeeping require read-before-write and key lookups that are inherently slower than a blind append-only insert.

tradeoffs.title: Latency
tradeoffs.note: Upserting into a keyed table incurs index maintenance and conflict resolution per row, adding write latency compared to a straight append.

tradeoffs.title: Maintainability
tradeoffs.note: Achieving idempotency demands disciplined natural or deterministic key design across every producer and stage, which is easy to get subtly wrong and costly to enforce.
